name: human-skeleton

description.en: 54 bones and bone groups of the human skeleton, from the skull to the foot. Front: the bone's everyday or anatomical name in English and Swedish; back: its Latin name in Terminologia Anatomica (TA98). Compiled from Wikidata, Svensk MeSH and the U.S. National Cancer Institute's SEER Training Modules, the Latin checked against TA98.

Sammanställd från Wikidata, Svensk MeSH och amerikanska National Cancer Institutes SEER Training Modules, med latinet kontrollerat mot TA98.

method: Research, drafting and cross-checking were done by AI agents (Claude, by Anthropic) at Anton Wiklund's direction, with machine checks and three review rounds by independent AI reviewers (factual accuracy; language and translation; licensing, attribution and documentation), logged under Quality control with every finding and how it was resolved (round 0 is the authoring agent's own source and machine check). The cards have not yet been reviewed by a human subject expert. Every value below was fetched on 2026-10-04; the exact queries and the code run on the downloads are listed under Queries. The raw responses and the authoring scripts were kept only in the authoring session's temporary working directory and are not preserved; rerunning the listed queries reproduces the data, though the live sources may have changed since.

Candidate list. The two SEER Training Module pages (U.S. National Cancer Institute, public domain) list the bones of the axial and appendicular skeleton. Their entries (cranial and facial bones, auditory ossicles, hyoid, vertebrae, sacrum, coccyx, sternum, ribs, clavicle, scapula, arm and leg bones, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges, hip bones, tarsals, metatarsals) were the starting list. It was extended with well-known bones and groups below that level: the atlas and axis, the auditory ossicles as a group, the vertebral column and the pelvis, the parts of the hip bone (ilium, ischium, pubis) and individual carpal and tarsal bones.

Wikidata. A SPARQL query looked up the Wikidata item of each candidate by English label, requiring a Terminologia Anatomica 98 ID (P1323); items it missed were found with wbsearchentities, choosing the item about the human bone (e.g. Q5283631 human mandible, Q9604 human skull, not the general Q16370 or Q13147). wbgetentities then fetched every item's en, sv and la labels and aliases and its P1323 statements.

Latin names (back). For each item, the TA98 entity page for its P1323 code was fetched from the TA98 online edition (ifaa.unifr.ch) and parsed for the Latin preferred term, Latin official synonym, English equivalent and English synonym. The card's Latin text follows TA98's naming: it is the TA98 Latin preferred term for the item's code, so TA98 decides which Latin form is on the back where several exist (Femur rather than Os femoris, Ossa metacarpi rather than Ossa metacarpalia). A single standardised anatomical term is a fact, not protected expression, so TA98 (all rights reserved) is listed as a verification source; no definitions, lists or other text were taken from it. Bracketed numbering in TA98 terms (e.g. "vertebrae cervicales [C I - C VII]", "atlas [C I]") is left out. TA98 prints the terms in lower case online; the cards capitalise the first letter, as the library brief does ("Femur"). Where TA98 gives two Latin terms (femur / os femoris, ossa carpi / ossa carpalia, os ilium / ilium) the preferred one is used. The same term is in Wikidata as a la label or alias for 44 of the 54 cards; for the other ten the Wikidata la label is missing (the skull), a synonym, a region name or malformed (see Quality control), and the term was confirmed in a second open source where one exists (a Wikidata en label or alias, a Wikidata sv alias, or a Svensk MeSH synonym or English entry term). For Ossa metacarpi and Ossa metatarsi no open source consulted has the exact preferred term (they give the TA98 official synonyms ossa metacarpalia and ossa metatarsalia, or the region names Metacarpus and Metatarsus), so these two backs rest on TA98 alone.

English names (front). Where English has an everyday name for the bone (thigh bone, kneecap, shinbone, calf bone, heel bone, collarbone, shoulder blade, breastbone, tailbone, backbone, cheekbone, upper jaw, lower jaw, hammer, anvil, stirrup), the front uses it; otherwise the English anatomical name (frontal bone, hip bone, scaphoid bone ...). Every English name is a Wikidata en label or alias except three (stirrup, and the plurals auditory ossicles and carpal bones), and each was cross-checked against the TA98 English equivalent or synonym, MeSH, the SEER list or the English Wikipedia introduction. "Stirrup" is common English vocabulary for the stapes; no open content source consulted lists it (Wikidata has only "stapes bone", Svensk MeSH no English synonym), and it rests on the English Wikipedia (verification). For six bones (humerus, radius, ulna, vomer, talus, pelvis) the established English name is the Latin name itself; these cards are kept for their Swedish names (review round 2 considered "Ankle bone" for the talus and "Upper arm bone" for the humerus and kept the anatomical names; see Quality control). The atlas and axis are given descriptively (first and second cervical vertebra), since their English names are also the Latin ones.

Swedish names (front). The Swedish name is the Wikidata sv label or alias when it agrees with the Svensk MeSH 2026 term or synonym (Karolinska Institutets Universitetsbibliotek, CC0), compared case-insensitively. Where the two disagree or one is missing, the name was chosen from the open sources and confirmed in the Swedish Wikipedia (verification): skalle (MeSH), underkäke (MeSH), plogben (MeSH synonym), ärtben (MeSH), sittben (MeSH), första/andra halskotan (MeSH), handlovens båtben (MeSH), fotens båtben (MeSH synonym "Båtben i foten", sv.wikipedia "Fotens båtben"), tårben, hakben, mellanhandsben, fotrotsben and tärningsben (Wikidata), bröstkotor and ländkotor (Svensk MeSH plurals of the Wikidata singulars). Swedish names are written in lower case as common nouns; the three ear ossicles are given in the definite form (hammaren, städet, stigbygeln) as Wikidata, Svensk MeSH for städet and the Swedish Wikipedia name them, since the indefinite forms name tools; the other bones are in the indefinite form as in the brief (lårben), except the atlas and axis, which are named with an ordinal and so take the definite form, as Svensk MeSH and the Swedish Wikipedia do (första halskotan, andra halskotan). Groups are in the plural (halskotor, revben, handlovsben).

Back notes. A short note on each card says where the bone is or how it is also called, in plain wording written for the deck. Each fact in a note was checked against a Svensk MeSH scope note (KIB's Swedish, or NLM's English one in the same download) where one states it, against the Swedish or English Wikipedia, or against the SEER count, and the supporting sentence is quoted in the card's evidence (for the notes of the atlas, axis, sacrum, maxilla, mandible, vomer, ethmoid, hyoid, lunate, hamate, femur, metacarpal, tarsal and metatarsal cards these quotes were added in review rounds 1-4). Counts that vary between people or sources (the number of bones in the pelvis, the number of fused coccygeal vertebrae) were left out, and the rib note says "most people". Where the sources disagree on a note's fact (the English Wikipedia puts the metatarsals in the midfoot, its Tarsus article and anatomy teaching put them in the forefoot), the note avoids the disputed term.

Cross-check. A script (gen.py, run in the authoring session's temporary working directory and not preserved) built each card's evidence from the saved raw data only: the Wikidata labels and P1323 values, the TA98 fields, the Svensk MeSH terms and synonyms, the SEER list item and the Wikipedia quote, asserting that each quoted text occurs in the saved page. For each card it added Wikidata checks for the P1323 code and for every en, sv and la label or alias that equals the card's text apart from capitalisation, using Wikidata's own spelling; every side that has no such label was logged as a finding in round 0 with how it was resolved. The builder re-runs all checks against live Wikidata. After the review rounds, the added evidence was written by a second script (also not preserved) that asserted every new quote against the saved Svensk MeSH tables and Wikipedia texts in the same way.

Uniqueness. Every front is unique in English and in Swedish and every Latin back is unique, so the deck is studied in both directions. Where Swedish uses one name for two bones (båtben for both the scaphoid of the wrist and the navicular of the foot), the fronts are qualified as Svensk MeSH and the Swedish Wikipedia do (handlovens båtben, fotens båtben).
selection: 54 cards: the bones and bone groups that the SEER Training Module lists of the axial and appendicular skeleton name (except the phalanges and the palatine bone and inferior nasal concha, see below), plus the atlas, axis, auditory ossicles as a group, vertebral column, pelvis, the three parts of the hip bone, four carpal bones (scaphoid, lunate, pisiform, hamate) and four tarsal bones (talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid). A bone was included only if it has a TA98 code, a TA98 Latin preferred term, an English name and a Swedish name confirmed in two sources. Left out: the phalanges, because TA98 gives the same Latin term (ossa digitorum, phalanges) for the fingers and the toes, so the back would not identify one card; the palatine bone, because the Swedish "gomben" is in Svensk MeSH only as a synonym of the hard palate, not the bone; the inferior nasal concha (Swedish only in the plural group "näsmusslor" in MeSH, no Wikidata sv label); the capitate, triquetrum, trapezium and trapezoid, whose Swedish names vary between sources (Wikidata gives Latin or "lilla mångkantiga benet", the Swedish Wikipedia "huvudbenet", "pyramidbenet", "trapetsbenet", "trapetslika benet", MeSH Latin); the three cuneiform bones, whose names differ only by medial, intermediate and lateral and which Svensk MeSH has only as the group "Kilformade ben"; the rib cage (TA98 cavea thoracis has no Latin label in Wikidata or Swedish synonym in MeSH to confirm it); and sesamoid bones other than the kneecap and the pisiform, whose number varies between people. Individual ribs, vertebrae by number and the bones' parts (processes, heads, sutures) are out of scope.

rounds.lens: Source cross-check and Wikidata machine checks
rounds.summary: Every card has evidence from Wikidata (content), the TA98 entity page (verification) and at least one of Svensk MeSH, SEER and the Swedish or English Wikipedia. 191 Wikidata checks (194 after the three added in review round 3, 196 after the two added in round 4): the TA98 ID (P1323) of 53 items and every en, sv and la label or alias that equals the card's text apart from case. The 24 card sides with no such Wikidata label are listed below with how they were resolved; the Latin always follows TA98's preferred term, never a disagreeing Wikidata label. Further discrepancies between the sources, and conventions chosen, follow. Not yet reviewed by a human subject expert.

findings.issue: Sources differ on which bones make up the pelvis: sv.wikipedia's introduction names four (both hip bones, sacrum, coccyx), its body text three; the hip bone article in en.wikipedia includes the coccyx.
findings.resolution: The back note does not list the bones ("The bony ring between the spine and the thigh bones").

findings.issue: The number of ribs varies between people (cervical and missing ribs).
findings.resolution: Back note says "Most people have twelve pairs" (sv.wikipedia: "De flesta människor har 24 revben").

findings.issue: Capitalisation differs between the sources: TA98 online and some Wikidata labels are lower case ("os zygomaticum", "vertebrae thoracicae"), many Wikidata sv labels are capitalised ("Hjässben", "Okben", "Stigbygeln").
findings.resolution: Cards use one convention (English sentence case, Swedish lower case, Latin initial capital). Labels are compared case-insensitively; each check uses Wikidata's own spelling, so the report may show a check that differs from the card only in case.

findings.issue: The SEER axial page lists "Platine (2)", a misspelling of palatine.
